lesson_title: Bytecode and Decompiling; NFT Wash Trading

metadata.note: No assigned reading for this lesson; every question is grounded in a visible slide.

lectures.title: Bytecode, NFT Wash Trading - lesson synthesis

questions.question_stem: An agent gives you a contract address with no published source. What does the chain itself hold for that contract?
questions.correct_answer: Runtime bytecode at the address; the source exists only if someone published it.
incorrect_answers: The Solidity source and its comments, stored with the bytecode when it is deployed.
A decompiled version that the node builds the first time the contract is called.
Only a hash of the code, so the bytecode itself must come from the deployer.
questions.explanation: The chain stores EVM bytecode at the address. Source code stays with the author unless someone uploads it to a verification service, so an analyst often starts from bytecode alone.
questions.lesson_block: The chain stores bytecode, not source

specific_source.anchor: The chain stores bytecode, not source

questions.question_stem: A verifier reports an exact match for a contract. What does that tell you?
questions.correct_answer: The published source compiles to this exact bytecode; it says nothing about safety.
incorrect_answers: The contract was audited and found safe, because a match means the code was reviewed.
The author is identified, because the verifier checks the deployer's account first.
The code behaves as its comments describe, because comments are tested against it.
questions.explanation: Verification means a service recompiled the source and got the bytecode the chain holds. It shows the source produces this code, not that the code is safe or who wrote it.
questions.lesson_block: Verified source: a match someone checked

specific_source.anchor: Verified source: a match someone checked

questions.question_stem: How is a 4-byte function selector made?
questions.correct_answer: It is the first four bytes of the Keccak-256 hash of the function's name and argument types.
incorrect_answers: It is the first four bytes of the contract's address, so each contract has its own selectors.
It is the first four bytes of a hash of the caller's address and the call's arguments.
It is a number the author assigns to every function by hand when the contract is compiled.
questions.explanation: The selector comes from the hash of the signature, such as transfer(address,uint256). Nothing about the contract or caller goes into it.

questions.question_stem: Two unrelated token contracts both have a function with the signature transfer(address,uint256). How do their selectors compare?
questions.correct_answer: They are identical, because the selector comes from the signature alone, not the contract.
incorrect_answers: They differ, because each contract's address is hashed into all of its own selectors.
They match only when the same author wrote both contracts and deployed them together.
They differ, because the selector depends on the block where each one was deployed.
questions.explanation: The same signature gives the same selector everywhere, which is why 0xa9059cbb reads as transfer on any token.

questions.question_stem: A signature database returns approve(address,uint256) for the selector a transaction used. What may the analyst conclude?
questions.correct_answer: A name someone registered for that selector; what happened still needs the logs.
incorrect_answers: The contract granted a spending approval, because the database confirms what was done.
The function is safe to call, because a registered signature has been reviewed.
The contract's source is verified, because databases list only verified contracts.
questions.explanation: A lookup gives a name that people submitted, a lead. It does not show what the contract's code does with those four bytes, so confirm from logs and balance changes.
questions.lesson_block: Looking up a selector: a name, not proof

specific_source.anchor: Looking up a selector: a name, not proof

questions.question_stem: Why can a selector lookup return more than one signature?
questions.correct_answer: Four bytes leave room for different signatures to share a selector, and entries are user-submitted.
incorrect_answers: Each function has one selector per compiler version, and the database lists every version of it.
Argument names are part of a signature, so each naming gets registered as its own separate entry.
Databases merge entries from several chains whose hash functions differ, so one selector repeats.
questions.explanation: Selectors are only four bytes, so collisions happen; Foundry's linter even reports proxy and implementation functions sharing one. Treat the name as a lead.
questions.lesson_block: Looking up a selector: a name, not proof

questions.question_stem: Which of these can a decompiler not recover from bytecode?
questions.correct_answer: The comments, the author's intent, and the names of variables and functions.
incorrect_answers: The functions, listed by their four-byte selectors, with one entry for each one.
The storage slots that the code reads and the slots that it writes to.
The calls the code makes to other contracts, and each call's target address.
questions.explanation: Names, comments and intent were never in the bytecode, so no tool can recover them. Functions by selector, storage access and call targets are usually recovered, though types can be wrong.
questions.lesson_block: A decompiler rebuilds structure, not intent

specific_source.anchor: A decompiler rebuilds structure, not intent

questions.question_stem: Decompiled output has the line require(msg.sender == storage[1]). What can the analyst say?
questions.correct_answer: The function runs for one caller only, whose address sits in slot 1, which you still need to read.
incorrect_answers: The function is limited to the contract's owner, since the tool names the variable storage[1] for you.
The function runs for any caller, since require checks only the caller's token balance at the time.
The slot holds the deployer, as storage[1] is always set at once when a contract is created.
questions.explanation: The tool made up the names; storage[1] is only a slot. The body restricts the function to one caller, but who that is needs a read of the slot.

specific_source.anchor: Decompiled code, as an analyst reads it

questions.question_stem: Decompiled code alone shows a contract moving tokens to a fixed address. How sure is that reading?
questions.correct_answer: Moderate at best, as decompilers err; verified source plus logs make it High.
incorrect_answers: High, because a decompiler restores the original source, as verified code does.
Low, because bytecode cannot support a finding at all until the source is found.
High, because code shows what can happen, so logs would add nothing more to it.
questions.explanation: The course scale puts decompiled code alone at Moderate at best. Code says what can happen and logs say what did; with both, still Moderate, since the decompiler can misread; with exact-match source and logs, High.

questions.question_stem: What makes a sale a wash trade?
questions.correct_answer: The seller is on both sides, so ownership barely changes but a price is logged.
incorrect_answers: The price is far above the collection's usual sales, so the demand is invented by it.
The token is sold twice in one day by wallets that never traded before that day.
The marketplace charges no fee on the sale, so the seller risks no loss whatever.
questions.explanation: Chainalysis defines wash trading as a transaction in which the seller is on both sides. The sale changes no real ownership, yet the marketplace records a price and volume others read as demand.
questions.lesson_block: Wash trading: the seller on both sides

specific_source.anchor: Wash trading: the seller on both sides

questions.question_stem: LooksRare paid LOOKS tokens as a share of platform trading volume. Why did that encourage wash trading?
questions.correct_answer: Trading with yourself raised recorded volume and earned tokens, even if the price never moved.
incorrect_answers: Self-trades were taxed less than ordinary sales, so they were cheaper to run for the owner.
Rewards went only to the highest bidder, so a rival bid had to be faked for each sale.
Rewards were paid on private sales, which cannot be seen and so cannot be checked later.
questions.explanation: The rewards were a percentage of total trading volume, so a seller trading with their own wallets earned tokens. The trading rewards were discontinued as of September 2023.

questions.question_stem: Wallet B bought NFT #7 from wallet A, but B's first incoming ETH came from A's funder. What does that show?
questions.correct_answer: B was funded by the seller's side, so it is not a separate buyer; the sale was self-financed.
incorrect_answers: B is a friend of A, because only friends ever fund one another's wallets and nobody else does.
The sale was real, because B paid with ETH that B already held when the sale took place.
A and B are the same person, because shared funding proves a single owner, and nothing else fits.
questions.explanation: Chainalysis's marker is a buyer funded by the selling address or by the seller's own funder. Shared funding ties the two together, though it does not by itself prove one person.
questions.lesson_block: Self-financed: follow the buyer's money back

specific_source.anchor: Self-financed: follow the buyer's money back

questions.question_stem: An NFT moves from wallet A to wallet B with a Transfer log but no payment and no marketplace call. Is it a wash trade?
questions.correct_answer: Not yet: with no sale it may be one person moving a token between wallets.
incorrect_answers: Yes, because any transfer between two linked wallets is a wash trade in itself.
Yes, at High confidence, since with no payment the seller paid himself here.
No, because wash trading needs three or more wallets and this is a single hop.
questions.explanation: A wash trade needs a sale. A Transfer log with no payment and no marketplace call is the own-wallet look-alike; check the payment and the funding before using the label.
